summary_html: Agency **files a court petition** to open a **dependency** (or similar) case. Federal funding frameworks (IV-E/ASFA) link court oversight, reasonable-efforts findings, and permanency timelines to downstream actions.

- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal review of court/agency performance measures

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Department of Health & Rehabilitative Services v. M.B.
key_cases.holding: A child's out-of-court statements that satisfy section 90.803(23)'s reliability safeguards are admissible as substantive evidence in a dependency hearing even when they are inconsistent with the child's in-court testimony, and dependency itself is proved by a preponderance of the evidence.
key_cases.relevance: When the agency files a dependency petition, M.B. governs what proof it may use and confirms the preponderance standard at adjudication.
key_cases.quote: are admissible as substantive evidence in a dependency hearing once they have satisfied the stringent reliability safeguards established in section 90.803(23) and refined in our prior case law

key_cases.case_name: R.F. v. Florida Department of Children & Families
key_cases.holding: Proof that a parent sexually abused one child does not by itself establish that a sibling is dependent; the court must examine all the circumstances to decide whether the parent poses a substantial risk of imminent abuse or neglect to the other child.
key_cases.relevance: R.F. governs the sufficiency of a dependency petition that alleges prospective abuse or neglect of a sibling.
key_cases.quote: While the commission of such an act may be highly relevant, it is not automatically dispositive of the issue of dependency.

key_cases.court: District Court of Appeal of Florida, Fourth District
key_cases.holding: Treating the mother's appeal of a family court judge's sua sponte dependency shelter order as a certiorari petition, the court granted relief and remanded because she was given no opportunity to be heard or present evidence at the shelter hearing.
key_cases.relevance: The case shows what a court must do before shelter findings under section 39.402 can stand as the opening of a dependency case.
key_cases.quote: We treat the mother's appeal as a petition for writ of certiorari, grant the petition, and remand with directions.

key_cases.holding: Indigent parents have a constitutional right to appointed counsel whenever the proceeding can result in permanent loss of parental custody; in other dependency proceedings the right is determined case by case.
key_cases.relevance: When the agency files a petition that can end in permanent loss of custody, D.B. requires the court to appoint counsel for indigent parents.
key_cases.quote: We find that a constitutional right to counsel necessarily arises where the proceedings can result in permanent loss of parental custody.

key_cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services of Durham County
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Federal Constitution does not require appointed counsel in every parental termination proceeding; whether due process requires counsel is decided case by case by the trial court, subject to appellate review.
key_cases.relevance: Lassiter sets the federal floor for counsel once a petition that may end parental rights is filed; Florida's In re D.B. goes further.
key_cases.quote: leave the decision whether due process calls for the appointment of counsel for indigent parents in termination proceedings to be answered in the first instance by the trial court

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: Illinois could not presume unwed fathers unfit and make their children wards of the State without a hearing; due process entitled Stanley to a hearing on his parental fitness, and denying him the hearing afforded all other parents denied him equal protection.
key_cases.relevance: Stanley is the foundational federal holding that a petition which will take a parent's children cannot be resolved without an individualized hearing on that parent's fitness.
key_cases.quote: as a matter of due process of law, Stanley was entitled to a hearing on his fitness as a parent before his children were taken from him
